points_json.example: At a noisy party you can follow one friend's voice while ignoring all other conversations around you.
points_json.point: Selective attention is the ability to focus on one input while ignoring others. Cherry (1953) studied this with dichotic listening — different messages played in each ear — and found people could shadow one message while barely noticing the other.

points_json.example: You suddenly hear your name mentioned across a crowded room even though you were not listening to that conversation.
points_json.point: The cocktail party effect shows attention is not a perfect wall. Important or personally relevant information, like your own name, can break through even when you are focused elsewhere.

points_json.example: A student tries to text a friend while the teacher explains a new formula, and remembers neither the text nor the formula.
points_json.point: Divided attention means splitting focus between tasks. Performance drops sharply when both tasks need thinking. Texting while studying is not true multitasking — the brain rapidly switches, and both tasks suffer.

points_json.example: An airport security officer watches X-ray screens for hours, catching a hidden knife in the tenth bag.
points_json.point: Sustained attention (vigilance) is keeping focus over long periods. Performance usually declines with time — this vigilance decrement is why air-traffic controllers and security staff take regular breaks.

points_json.example: Half the viewers counting basketball passes fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene.
points_json.point: Inattentional blindness (Simons and Chabris, 1999) proves we miss obvious things when attention is elsewhere. Attention is a limited resource — focusing hard on one thing makes us blind to others.

points_json.example: A driver on a hands-free phone call misses a red light she would normally see instantly.
points_json.point: Attention has strict capacity limits. Even hands-free phone use while driving raises crash risk as much as drunk driving, because the conversation consumes the attention needed for the road.

points_json.example: A goalkeeper watches the striker's hips, not the ball, to predict where the shot will go.
points_json.point: Experts attend differently from beginners. With practice, attention becomes automatic for routine parts of a task, freeing mental resources. This automaticity is why skilled drivers can chat while beginners cannot.

summary: How the mind picks one thing out of a noisy world — and what it misses while doing so. The classic experiments behind attention research, in simple words.
title: Attention and Selective Focus

points_json.example: You repeat a phone number in your head — 4-3-2-8-9-1-5 — until you can type it into your mobile.
points_json.point: Working memory is the mental workspace where you hold and manipulate information for seconds. Unlike passive short-term storage, it actively processes — you can repeat, rearrange, and calculate with what you hold.

points_json.example: Remembering the route a friend describes: turn left at the bakery, then right at the mosque — you picture the turns in your mind.
points_json.point: Baddeley's model (1974) has four parts. The visuospatial sketchpad holds images and locations, like a mental map. The phonological loop holds speech-based sounds through silent rehearsal.

points_json.example: While cooking, you keep the recipe steps in mind, watch the pot, and answer your child's question at the same time.
points_json.point: The central executive is the boss of working memory — it directs attention, switches between tasks, and decides what matters. The episodic buffer (added 2000) links working memory with long-term memory into one conscious experience.

points_json.example: The number 0301-2345678 is easier to remember as three chunks: 0301, 234, 5678.
points_json.point: Miller's famous 7 plus or minus 2 is the capacity limit — but chunking beats it. Grouping items into meaningful units lets experts remember far more. A chess master remembers whole board positions as single chunks.

points_json.example: A waiter takes a 6-person order without writing anything, but forgets it completely after serving.
points_json.point: Without rehearsal, working memory fades in about 15–30 seconds (Peterson and Peterson, 1959). Distraction wipes it fast — which is why the waiter forgets once interrupted.

points_json.example: Students who solve math problems in their heads while remembering the question score worse than those who write steps down.
points_json.point: Complex span tasks measure working memory by combining storage with processing. Working memory capacity predicts reasoning, reading comprehension, and exam performance better than IQ alone in many studies.

points_json.example: A child with weak working memory struggles to follow three-step instructions: take your bag, wash your hands, sit down.
points_json.point: Working memory develops through childhood and shrinks with age. It is linked to ADHD and learning difficulties. Training programs exist, but benefits rarely transfer beyond the trained task itself.

summary: The mind's mental workspace — Baddeley's model, why you forget phone numbers, and how chunking expands your limits.
title: Working Memory in Depth

points_json.example: You remember your first day at school — the smell of new books, your mother's hand — but also know that Paris is the capital of France.
points_json.point: Long-term memory splits into explicit (conscious) and implicit (unconscious) systems. Explicit memory further divides: episodic memory stores personal life events, semantic memory stores facts and general knowledge.

points_json.example: You ride a bicycle after ten years without thinking about balance or pedaling.
points_json.point: Procedural memory is skill memory — riding a bike, typing, swimming. It is implicit: you perform it automatically and often cannot explain how. Patient H.M. proved it survives even when episodic memory is destroyed.

points_json.example: After seeing the word DOCTOR, you recognize the word NURSE faster than the word BREAD.
points_json.point: Priming is implicit memory at work — recent exposure makes related information easier to process, without conscious recall. Advertisers and test designers exploit priming constantly.

points_json.example: A song from your childhood instantly brings back the feeling of summer holidays at your grandmother's house.
points_json.point: Tulving's encoding specificity principle: memory works best when retrieval conditions match learning conditions. Context — place, mood, even smell — acts as a retrieval cue. Studying in the same room as the exam can help.

points_json.example: You learned French words with pictures last month and still remember them, but forgot the list you only repeated aloud.
points_json.point: Levels of processing (Craik and Lockhart, 1972): deep, meaningful encoding creates stronger memories than shallow repetition. Elaborative rehearsal — connecting new facts to what you know — beats rote memorization.

points_json.example: A witness confidently identifies the wrong person because the real criminal's face blended with a bystander seen later.
points_json.point: Memory is reconstructive, not a video recording. Every recall rebuilds the memory, and it can change. This is why eyewitness testimony is unreliable and why memories feel certain even when wrong.

points_json.example: Your grandmother remembers her wedding day vividly but cannot recall what she ate yesterday.
points_json.point: Older, well-consolidated memories resist forgetting better than recent ones — Ribot's law. Emotional memories, especially, are strengthened by the amygdala and feel exceptionally vivid.

summary: Episodic, semantic, procedural — the separate filing systems of long-term memory, and why recall rebuilds rather than replays.
title: Long-Term Memory Systems

points_json.example: A student memorizes 50 vocabulary words on Sunday and remembers only 15 by Friday without revision.
points_json.point: Ebbinghaus (1885) memorized nonsense syllables and plotted the forgetting curve — memory drops steeply within the first hour, then levels off. Most forgetting happens fast; what survives the first day tends to last.

points_json.example: You keep calling your new teacher by your old teacher's name for the first month of school.
points_json.point: Proactive interference: old learning blocks new learning. Retroactive interference is the reverse — new learning blocks old, like forgetting last year's password after setting a new one.

points_json.example: You cannot recall a colleague's name at the office, but it pops into your head the moment you see her at the market where you first met.
points_json.point: Retrieval failure theory: the memory exists but lacks the right cue. Tulving's encoding specificity explains this — the market matches the original encoding context, unlocking the name.

points_json.example: An old song suddenly returns a childhood memory you had not thought about in twenty years.
points_json.point: Decay theory says memories fade with time if unused, like a path overgrown without walking. But many researchers argue memories rarely vanish — the problem is usually failed retrieval, not true erasure.

points_json.example: A trauma survivor cannot recall the worst moments of an accident, though doctors find no brain damage.
points_json.point: Motivated forgetting: Freud proposed repression pushes painful memories out of awareness. Modern research confirms suppression-induced forgetting — deliberately avoiding a memory weakens it — though true repression remains debated.

points_json.example: You walk into the kitchen and completely forget why you came.
points_json.point: Schacter's seven sins of memory include absentmindedness — forgetting caused by divided attention at encoding. You never properly stored the reason, so there is nothing to retrieve.

points_json.example: A medical student reviews anatomy with spaced flashcards and still remembers it years later as a doctor.
points_json.point: The antidote to forgetting is spaced retrieval practice — testing yourself at expanding intervals. Each successful retrieval strengthens the memory far more than re-reading the same page.

summary: Why memories fade — Ebbinghaus's curve, interference, retrieval failure, and the science-backed ways to fight forgetting.
title: Forgetting: Theories and Research

points_json.example: A witness who read a news report saying the car was blue later swears in court the car was blue — but it was actually green.
points_json.point: The misinformation effect (Loftus, 1978): false details learned after an event get woven into the memory of the event itself. Post-event information rewrites what we believe we saw.

points_json.example: Asking 'how fast were the cars going when they smashed?' makes witnesses estimate higher speeds than asking about when they 'hit.'
points_json.point: Leading questions distort memory. Loftus showed the verb used — smashed, collided, bumped, hit — changed speed estimates and even created false memories of broken glass that was never there.

points_json.example: In the famous lost-in-the-mall study, a quarter of participants came to remember a childhood event that never happened.
points_json.point: Entire false memories can be implanted. With suggestive storytelling, people recalled being lost in a shopping mall as children — complete with vivid details — for an event their families confirmed never occurred.

points_json.example: You clearly remember locking the door, but you are actually remembering yesterday's locking mixed with today's rush.
points_json.point: Source misattribution: we remember the information but confuse where it came from. Dreams, imagination, photos, and stories all become tangled sources that feel like real experience.

points_json.example: A witness picks an innocent person from a lineup and says 'I'm 100% sure' — yet DNA later proves her wrong.
points_json.point: Eyewitness confidence does not equal accuracy. Stress, weapons focus, cross-race identification, and suggestive lineups all damage accuracy while confidence stays high — a deadly combination in courtrooms.

points_json.example: The Innocence Project has freed hundreds of wrongly convicted people, most convicted on eyewitness testimony later disproved by DNA.
points_json.point: Real-world stakes are enormous: mistaken eyewitness identification is the leading cause of wrongful convictions worldwide. Sequential lineups and blind administration reduce — but cannot eliminate — the risk.

points_json.example: People who imagined breaking a window as children later rated it more likely to have really happened.
points_json.point: Imagination inflation shows that vividly imagining an event increases belief it occurred. Therapists, interviewers, and even our own daydreams can accidentally manufacture memories this way.

summary: How completely false memories form — Loftus's groundbreaking research and why eyewitness testimony sends innocent people to prison.
title: False Memories and Eyewitness Testimony

points_json.example: After his 1953 brain operation, H.M. could not remember the doctor who had examined him just minutes earlier.
points_json.point: Henry Molaison (H.M.) had brain surgery to stop severe epilepsy. Surgeons removed parts of his temporal lobes, including the hippocampus. He developed severe anterograde amnesia — unable to form new long-term memories — while his childhood memories stayed intact.

points_json.example: H.M. learned a mirror-drawing task better each day, yet every day insisted he had never done it before.
points_json.point: H.M.'s famous discovery: his procedural memory worked perfectly. He learned motor skills with practice but had zero conscious memory of the training. This proved skill memory and fact memory live in separate brain systems.

points_json.example: Clive Wearing, a musician, greets his wife joyfully every few minutes as if she just arrived — yet he can still play the piano beautifully.
points_json.point: Clive Wearing's viral encephalitis destroyed his hippocampus. He lives in a permanent present of seconds, constantly writing in his diary that he has 'just woken up.' Yet his musical skill memory survived, like H.M.'s.

points_json.example: Patient K.C. lost all personal memories after a motorcycle accident but could still learn new facts about the world.
points_json.point: K.C. showed the reverse pattern: episodic memory destroyed, semantic memory partly spared. Together with H.M., such cases proved episodic and semantic memory are genuinely different systems.

points_json.example: You remember almost nothing from before age three, though you surely experienced a great deal.
points_json.point: Infantile amnesia: adults cannot recall early childhood. The hippocampus is still maturing, and young children lack the language and self-concept needed to encode lasting autobiographical memories.

points_json.example: An amnesic patient who was once pricked by a pin hidden in a handshake later refused to shake that doctor's hand — without knowing why.
points_json.point: Implicit memory survives amnesia. Claparede's pin experiment showed emotional learning continues unconsciously — the patient avoided the handshake with no conscious memory of the pain.

points_json.example: Modern brain scans confirm the hippocampus is the gateway that consolidates new memories for long-term storage.
points_json.point: H.M.'s legacy reshaped neuroscience: memory is not one thing but many systems in different brain regions. His brain, donated to science, is still studied today through detailed digital slicing.

summary: Patient H.M. — the man who could not make new memories. The most famous case in psychology and what it taught us about memory systems.
title: Amnesia: Case Studies (H.M.)

points_json.example: A baby says 'ba-ba-ba' at six months, 'mama' at one year, and 'mama go' at eighteen months — the same sequence in every culture.
points_json.point: Language develops in universal stages: cooing (2 months), babbling (6 months), one-word holophrases (12 months), two-word telegraphic speech (18–24 months), then full sentences. Deaf babies babble with their hands in sign language.

points_json.example: A toddler says 'I goed to the park' and 'two foots' — applying rules she was never taught.
points_json.point: Overregularization proves children learn grammar rules, not just imitation. No one teaches 'goed' — the child applies the past-tense rule too broadly, showing an active rule-building mind.

points_json.example: Genie, isolated until age 13 with almost no language exposure, never developed normal grammar despite years of training.
points_json.point: The critical period hypothesis: language must be learned in childhood for full mastery. Cases like Genie suggest that after puberty, the brain loses its special readiness for first-language grammar.

points_json.example: Chomsky argued children learn language too fast, from too little data, for it to be pure imitation.
points_json.point: Chomsky proposed a Language Acquisition Device — an inborn capacity for grammar — and universal grammar shared by all languages. The poverty of the stimulus argument: children hear messy, incomplete speech yet extract perfect rules.

points_json.example: A mother naturally raises her pitch and slows down: 'Who's a gooood baby?' — and the baby babbles back happily.
points_json.point: Child-directed speech (motherese) — high pitch, slow tempo, exaggerated intonation — appears worldwide and helps babies segment sounds and learn words. Social interaction, not just exposure, drives learning.

points_json.example: Skinner showed pigeons could be shaped with rewards; he claimed children learn language the same way — through reinforcement.
points_json.point: Behaviorists credit imitation and reinforcement: parents smile at correct words and correct mistakes. But this cannot explain novel sentences — children produce phrases they never heard, like 'allgone sticky.'

points_json.example: A three-year-old narrates her play aloud: 'now dolly sleeps, shh' — talking to guide her own actions.
points_json.point: Vygotsky saw language as a social tool first. Private speech — children talking to themselves — becomes inner speech, the silent self-talk adults use for thinking and self-control.

summary: How babies go from babbling to sentences — stages, Chomsky vs Skinner, the critical period, and the mystery of grammar.
title: Language Acquisition

points_json.example: A bilingual child says 'I want leche' — mixing Spanish and English in one sentence without confusion.
points_json.point: Code-switching — mixing languages mid-sentence — follows strict grammatical rules and is a sign of skill, not confusion. Bilingual children keep their languages separate from very early on.

points_json.example: Brain scans show a second language learned in childhood uses the same brain areas as the first; late-learned languages use slightly different regions.
points_json.point: Age of acquisition shapes the brain. Early bilinguals process both languages in overlapping left-hemisphere areas. Late learners recruit additional regions, and rarely achieve a native accent.

points_json.example: Bialystok found bilingual patients developed dementia symptoms about 4–5 years later than monolingual patients.
points_json.point: Cognitive reserve: lifelong bilingualism may delay dementia symptoms. Managing two languages exercises executive control constantly — though recent studies debate how large this advantage really is.

points_json.example: A bilingual adult names pictures slightly slower in each language than a monolingual would in one.
points_json.point: There are costs too: bilinguals typically have smaller vocabularies in each language and slower word retrieval. The constant competition between languages creates a measurable processing cost.

points_json.example: A child understands her grandmother's Punjabi perfectly but answers only in English.
points_json.point: Receptive bilingualism — understanding without speaking — is common and still valuable. Language dominance can shift with environment; the childhood language may fade without use, called first-language attrition.

points_json.example: Bilinguals in one famous study were faster at ignoring distracting arrows in attention tests.
points_json.point: The proposed bilingual advantage in executive function — better inhibition and task-switching — made headlines but faces a replication crisis. Effects, if real, are small and depend on how often both languages are actually used.

points_json.example: An interpreter switches between languages all day, a workout no gym can match.
points_json.point: Simultaneous interpreters show extraordinary working memory and attention control. Their brains demonstrate extreme neuroplasticity — proof that intense language use physically reshapes cognition.

summary: Two languages, one brain — code-switching, the dementia-delay finding, and the debate over the bilingual advantage.
title: Bilingualism and the Brain

points_json.example: Asked to name a bird, most people say 'sparrow' or 'robin' — almost nobody says 'penguin' first.
points_json.point: Prototype theory (Rosch, 1975): categories form around a best example — the prototype. A robin is a prototypical bird; a penguin is a marginal member. Typicality affects how fast we recognize and name things.

points_json.example: A tomato is technically a fruit, but most people file it mentally under vegetables.
points_json.point: Classical theory said categories have strict defining features. Real categories are fuzzy — tomatoes, olives, and avocados blur the fruit-vegetable line. Membership is graded, not all-or-nothing.

points_json.example: You instantly know a poodle and a bulldog are both dogs, though they look very different.
points_json.point: Exemplar theory: we store specific examples, not abstract definitions. New items are judged by similarity to remembered exemplars. This explains how we categorize wildly different-looking members of one group.

points_json.example: People answer 'what is it?' fastest at the basic level — 'dog,' not 'animal' or 'golden retriever.'
points_json.point: Categories form hierarchies: superordinate (animal), basic (dog), subordinate (golden retriever). The basic level is special — learned first by children, named fastest, and richest in shared features.

points_json.example: A child calls every four-legged animal 'doggie' — including cats and goats.
points_json.point: Children overextend categories, then narrow them with experience. Concepts develop through encounters: each new dog refines the boundary of what counts as a dog.

points_json.example: Most people picture a chair with four legs and a back — even though beanbags and stools count as chairs.
points_json.point: Schemas are mental frameworks organizing knowledge about objects and situations. Scripts are schemas for events — your restaurant script tells you to wait, order, eat, then pay, in every new restaurant.

points_json.example: An expert birdwatcher sees a 'warbler' where a beginner just sees a 'bird.'
points_json.point: Expertise shifts the basic level downward. Experts categorize at more specific levels automatically — the birdwatcher's brain treats 'warbler' the way yours treats 'bird.'

summary: How the mind files the world — prototypes, fuzzy boundaries, hierarchies, and why a penguin is a bad bird.
title: Concepts and Categories

points_json.example: All humans are mortal. Socrates is human. Therefore, Socrates is mortal.
points_json.point: Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a guaranteed conclusion. If the premises are true and the logic valid, the conclusion must be true. Mathematics and formal logic run on deduction.

points_json.example: All observed swans are white, so the next swan will probably be white too — until a black swan appears.
points_json.point: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to general conclusions. It is powerful but never certain — one black swan in Australia destroyed centuries of 'all swans are white' certainty.

points_json.example: Valid: All cats are mammals; all mammals are animals; therefore all cats are animals. Invalid: All cats have tails; my dog has a tail; therefore my dog is a cat.
points_json.point: Validity is about form, not truth. An argument can be logically valid with false premises, or have true premises yet be invalid. People constantly confuse 'the conclusion sounds true' with 'the logic is valid.'

points_json.example: If it rains, the ground gets wet. It rained. Therefore the ground is wet — most people get this instantly.
points_json.point: Modus ponens (if P then Q; P; therefore Q) feels natural. But its twin, modus tollens (if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P), trips people up — showing reasoning depends on logical form, not just content.

points_json.example: People accept 'some dogs are pets, some pets are brown, therefore some dogs are brown' — which is logically invalid.
points_json.point: Belief bias: we judge arguments by believability of the conclusion instead of logical validity. When conclusions sound plausible, we stop checking the logic — a major source of everyday bad reasoning.

points_json.example: A doctor reasons: fever plus rash plus recent travel — most likely dengue, so order the dengue test first.
points_json.point: Abductive reasoning infers the best explanation — the logic of diagnosis and detective work. It is technically a form of induction: the likeliest cause, not a guaranteed one.

points_json.example: Wason's selection task: most people fail the abstract version but solve the identical drinking-age version instantly.
points_json.point: Content radically affects reasoning performance. Abstract logic puzzles defeat most people, yet the same logical structure embedded in a social rule (who may drink alcohol) becomes easy — evidence for specialized reasoning modules.

summary: Two engines of thought — deduction's certainty, induction's gamble, and why believable conclusions make us sloppy logicians.
title: Reasoning: Deductive vs Inductive

points_json.example: A smoker reads three articles doubting the smoking-cancer link and ignores fifty confirming it.
points_json.point: Confirmation bias: we seek, notice, and remember information that supports what we already believe. Wason's 2-4-6 task showed people test only confirming examples, rarely trying to disprove their own rule.

points_json.example: A shopkeeper first says a watch costs 50,000, then 'discounts' it to 20,000 — which suddenly feels cheap.
points_json.point: Anchoring: the first number we encounter drags all later judgments toward it, even when random. Tversky and Kahneman spun a rigged wheel, then asked about African UN membership — the random number still anchored answers.

points_json.example: After a plane crash fills the news, people fear flying — though driving to the airport is statistically far deadlier.
points_json.point: The availability heuristic: we judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, emotional events feel common; quiet, statistical killers feel rare.

points_json.example: A manager hires the candidate who went to her own university, feeling an instant, unexamined trust.
points_json.point: These three biases share a root: System 1 thinking (Kahneman) — fast, automatic, effortless. It handles most daily judgments brilliantly, but systematically misfires on statistics, randomness, and logic.

points_json.example: Doctors who first consider the common diagnosis often miss the rare disease, even when symptoms point to it.
points_json.point: In medicine, availability bias kills: dramatic recent cases dominate diagnosis. Checklists and structured second opinions exist precisely to force System 2 — slow, deliberate thinking — back into the process.

points_json.example: Investors buy stocks they have heard of repeatedly, mistaking familiarity for safety.
points_json.point: The availability heuristic drives markets: heavily covered companies feel safer, so money flows to famous stocks regardless of fundamentals. Mere exposure masquerades as evidence.

points_json.example: A debater only Googles phrases that support her side, then wonders why opponents seem irrational.
points_json.point: Fighting confirmation bias requires steelmanning — arguing the other side's best case — and pre-committing to what evidence would change your mind before you look.

summary: The mind's favorite traps, part one — confirmation, anchoring, and availability, with the classic experiments that exposed them.
title: Cognitive Biases Collection I

points_json.example: After an election, everyone claims they 'knew all along' who would win — though polls showed a dead heat.
points_json.point: Hindsight bias: after an outcome is known, it feels inevitable. 'I knew it all along' rewrites history — we forget our earlier uncertainty, which makes the world feel more predictable than it is.

points_json.example: A business book studies ten successful startups and concludes 'drop out of college' — ignoring the thousands of dropouts who failed.
points_json.point: Survivorship bias: we study only the winners. Failed companies, unpublished studies, and dead soldiers vanish from the sample, so success looks easier and its causes look clearer than they are.

points_json.example: A couple stays in a miserable marriage 'because we've already spent ten years together.'
points_json.point: The sunk cost fallacy: past investments — money, time, effort — should not affect future decisions, but they do. Rational choice looks forward; human choice clings to what is already spent.

points_json.example: Generals keep sending soldiers into a losing war because so many have already died — 'we can't let their sacrifice be in vain.'
points_json.point: Sunk cost thinking turns tragic at scale: the Concorde fallacy is named for the supersonic jet both governments kept funding long after it was clearly uneconomical, purely because of money already spent.

points_json.example: Students rate a boring lecture as more interesting after suffering through a harsh initiation to join the class.
points_json.point: Effort justification (Aronson and Mills, 1959): the harsher the initiation, the more people value the group. Our brains convert suffered costs into perceived value — the root of hazing and brand loyalty alike.

points_json.example: Hiring managers favor the candidate interviewed first thing Monday morning over identical ones seen Friday afternoon.
points_json.point: Related traps multiply: the primacy effect, the halo effect, and status quo bias all push judgments off-course. Naming a bias is the first step to dodging it — which is why collections like this matter.

points_json.example: A gambler who has lost all night doubles his bets, convinced a win 'must' come soon.
points_json.point: The gambler's fallacy — believing random events self-correct — pairs with sunk cost: losses already suffered demand 'just one more' bet. Casinos are architecturally designed around these exact biases.

summary: The mind's favorite traps, part two — hindsight, survivorship, and sunk cost, and how they quietly run businesses and wars.
title: Cognitive Biases Collection II

points_json.example: Guilford asked: how many uses can you list for a brick? Most say three; creative thinkers list thirty.
points_json.point: Divergent thinking generates many possible answers; convergent thinking narrows to one correct answer. Creativity needs both — wild generation followed by disciplined selection. Tests like Guilford's measure fluency, flexibility, and originality.

points_json.example: The Post-it note was born when a weak glue — a failed strong adhesive — met someone who saw a new use for it.
points_json.point: Wallas (1926) described four creative stages: preparation (learning the problem), incubation (unconscious processing), illumination (the aha moment), and verification (testing the idea). Breaks and sleep genuinely help — the mind works offline.

points_json.example: In Duncker's candle problem, most people fail to see a box as a candle holder — they see only a container for tacks.
points_json.point: Functional fixedness blocks creativity: we see objects only in their familiar roles. The candle problem is solved by seeing the tack box as a platform — a mental shift most people need a hint to make.

points_json.example: Children promised a reward for drawing produce less creative drawings than children who draw for fun.
points_json.point: Amabile's research: intrinsic motivation fuels creativity; expected rewards can crush it. People do their most original work when the task itself is the reward — autonomy and play beat prizes.

points_json.example: The Beatles played thousands of hours in Hamburg clubs before writing their masterpieces.
points_json.point: The 10,000-hour rule (Ericsson's deliberate practice research) is often oversimplified, but the core holds: deep expertise requires years of focused, feedback-driven practice. Creativity without craft rarely lasts.

points_json.example: Einstein called combinatory play — imagining riding a beam of light — the essence of his scientific thinking.
points_json.point: Creative minds combine distant ideas: Einstein merged physics with thought experiments, Darwin merged biology with Malthus's economics. Analogical thinking across domains is a hallmark of breakthrough creativity.

points_json.example: Brainstorming groups actually produce fewer ideas than the same people working alone, then pooling results.
points_json.point: Surprising finding: classic group brainstorming underperforms solitary idea generation due to production blocking and social loafing. Brainwriting — silent individual writing first — works far better.

summary: Where new ideas come from — divergent thinking, the candle problem, why rewards can kill creativity, and how breakthroughs really happen.
title: Creativity and Divergent Thinking

points_json.example: Close your eyes and count the windows in your childhood home — you mentally walk through it, scanning each room.
points_json.point: Kosslyn's scanning experiments showed mental images work like real pictures: the longer the distance across a memorized map, the longer the mental scan takes. Imagery preserves spatial layout.

points_json.example: Deciding which of two rotated shapes match takes longer the further one must be mentally rotated.
points_json.point: Shepard and Metzler (1971) found mental rotation time increases linearly with rotation angle — as if the mind physically turns the object. This proved imagery is depictive, like a picture, not just verbal description.

points_json.example: Memory champions memorize 100 digits by placing vivid images along a familiar street — the method of loci.
points_json.point: Imagery supercharges memory. The ancient method of loci — placing bizarre mental images along a familiar route — lets competitors memorize decks of cards in minutes. Vivid, strange images stick best.

points_json.example: A basketball player who mentally rehearses free throws improves almost as much as one who physically practices.
points_json.point: Mental practice works: athletes who vividly imagine perfect performance improve measurably. The brain's motor areas activate during imagery much as in real movement — practice without moving.

points_json.example: Some people cannot picture an apple at all — they know what it is, but see only blackness.
points_json.point: Aphantasia is the inability to form voluntary mental images, affecting a few percent of people. Many discover it only as adults — and live perfectly normal lives, proving imagery is useful but not essential.

points_json.example: Brain scans show imagining a scene activates the visual cortex almost as if you were seeing it.
points_json.point: The great imagery debate: Kosslyn argued images are picture-like in the brain; Pylyshyn argued they are propositional — language-like descriptions. Modern neuroscience sides mostly with Kosslyn: imagery reuses perceptual brain areas.

points_json.example: A student imagines the water cycle as a cartoon: sun drinking from a lake, clouds crying rain.
points_json.point: Dual coding (Paivio): information stored as both image and word is remembered better than either alone. Turning abstract material into mental pictures is one of the most powerful study techniques known.

summary: Pictures in the mind's eye — mental rotation, the memory palace, aphantasia, and why imagining practice improves real performance.
title: Mental Imagery

points_json.example: You stop yourself from shouting at a rude cashier, switch plans when it rains, and keep a phone number in mind while dialing.
points_json.point: Executive functions are the brain's control panel: inhibition (stopping impulses), shifting (switching tasks), and updating (refreshing working memory). Miyake's research shows these three core skills underlie all complex thought.

points_json.example: A four-year-old who can wait 15 minutes for two marshmallows instead of eating one now tends to do better years later in school.
points_json.point: Mischel's marshmallow test became famous for linking childhood self-control to later success. Later replications show the effect is real but smaller — and heavily influenced by family background and trust.

points_json.example: A teenager knows texting while driving is dangerous — and does it anyway when friends are watching.
points_json.point: The prefrontal cortex, home of executive functions, matures into the mid-twenties. Adolescents have adult-level reasoning but child-level impulse control — especially with peers present, when reward circuits overpower control.

points_json.example: Adults with ADHD often describe their minds as having thirty browser tabs open with music playing.
points_json.point: Executive dysfunction is central to ADHD: difficulty inhibiting distractions, organizing tasks, and managing time. It is not a knowledge problem — it is a performance problem of the brain's management system.

points_json.example: After frontal lobe damage, Phineas Gage changed from responsible to impulsive — his intellect intact, his self-control gone.
points_json.point: The prefrontal cortex is the seat of executive function. Damage here, as in the famous 1848 case of Phineas Gage, can leave memory and IQ untouched while destroying planning, judgment, and social behavior.

points_json.example: Brain-training games make you better at those games — but rarely improve real-life attention or memory.
points_json.point: The far-transfer debate: executive function training shows near transfer (better at similar tasks) but weak far transfer to daily life. Aerobic exercise and good sleep currently show stronger real-world benefits.

points_json.example: A surgeon follows a mental checklist: verify patient, verify site, count instruments — every single time.
points_json.point: Experts offload executive demands onto routines and checklists. Externalizing control — writing things down, building habits — is the most reliable way to compensate for limited executive resources.

summary: The brain's control panel — inhibition, shifting, updating, the marshmallow test, and why teenagers can't resist peer pressure.
title: Executive Functions

points_json.example: A student finishes reading a chapter and thinks 'I've got this' — then blanks on every question in the exam.
points_json.point: Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking — monitoring and controlling learning. Judgments of learning are often wrong: fluency from re-reading feels like mastery but predicts almost nothing about exam performance.

points_json.example: An actor's name sits on the tip of your tongue — you know you know it, and feel it coming.
points_json.point: The tip-of-the-tongue state and feeling-of-knowing show metacognition in action: we can accurately sense that knowledge exists even when we cannot retrieve it. The monitor works even when retrieval fails.

points_json.example: In one study, the lowest-scoring students overestimated their performance by the widest margin.
points_json.point: The Dunning-Kruger effect: the least competent are the most overconfident, because the same lack of skill that causes errors prevents recognizing them. True experts, aware of complexity, often underestimate themselves.

points_json.example: A medical student who practices with past papers outperforms one who only re-reads notes — and predicts her score more accurately.
points_json.point: Testing beats re-reading: the testing effect shows retrieval practice both strengthens memory and calibrates metacognition. Self-testers learn what they actually know versus what merely feels familiar.

points_json.example: A chess beginner spends equal time on all positions; a master focuses study on her weakest openings.
points_json.point: Good metacognition directs study efficiently: allocate time to unlearned material, not comfortable review. Poor monitors waste hours re-reading what they already know.

points_json.example: Flavell, who coined the term in 1979, found children develop awareness of their own memory around age five.
points_json.point: Metacognition develops in childhood: young children are wildly overconfident about memory and knowledge. By adolescence, monitoring improves — though overconfidence never fully disappears, even in experts.

points_json.example: A writer sets a timer, drafts without editing, then revises — planning, monitoring, and evaluating in sequence.
points_json.point: The metacognitive cycle — plan, monitor, evaluate — applies to any complex task. Explicitly asking 'what's my plan? am I on track? did it work?' measurably improves problem-solving.

summary: Thinking about thinking — why re-reading feels like learning but isn't, the Dunning-Kruger effect, and how to study smarter.
title: Metacognition: Thinking About Thinking

points_json.example: A student trying to learn from a diagram on page 12 while its explanation sits on page 15 keeps flipping back and forth, exhausted.
points_json.point: Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller, 1988): working memory is tiny, so instruction must respect its limits. Every learning task carries intrinsic load (the difficulty itself), extraneous load (bad design), and germane load (useful mental effort).

points_json.example: A beginner learns algebra faster by studying worked examples than by solving problems from scratch.
points_json.point: The worked-example effect: novices learn more from studying fully solved examples than from struggling through problems. Problem-solving burns working memory on search instead of learning the underlying pattern.

points_json.example: Placing labels directly on a diagram beats a legend below it — students learn faster and remember more.
points_json.point: The split-attention effect: when related information is separated in space or time, learners waste mental effort integrating it. Integrated formats — labels on diagrams, subtitles with video — cut extraneous load.

points_json.example: Students learn the water cycle better from animation plus narration than from animation plus on-screen text.
points_json.point: The modality effect: using both ears and eyes (spoken words with visuals) expands effective working memory versus overloading one channel. Two channels carry more than one — if they complement rather than duplicate.

points_json.example: Advanced students actually learn worse from worked examples that beginners need — they get bored and disengaged.
points_json.point: The expertise reversal effect: techniques that help novices hinder experts. As knowledge grows into schemas in long-term memory, heavy guidance becomes redundant and even harmful.

points_json.example: A 40-minute lecture with no break leaves students remembering almost nothing from the last 20 minutes.
points_json.point: Attention and working memory fatigue fast. Segmenting — breaking content into short chunks with pauses — restores capacity. The brain consolidates during breaks, not during continuous input.

points_json.example: An app that teaches with tiny daily lessons, instant feedback, and no clutter outperforms a dense textbook chapter.
points_json.point: Good design follows the theory: minimize clutter, integrate related elements, use audio with visuals, and fade guidance as learners advance. Most failed e-learning violates these principles.

summary: Why your brain crashes like an overloaded computer — Sweller's theory of working memory limits and how good teaching respects them.
title: Cognitive Load Theory

points_json.example: Most people choose a guaranteed 3,000 over an 80% chance of 4,000 — but prefer an 80% chance of losing 4,000 over a certain loss of 3,000.
points_json.point: Prospect Theory (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979) replaced pure rationality: we evaluate outcomes as gains and losses from a reference point, not as final wealth. Losing 100 hurts about twice as much as gaining 100 pleases — loss aversion.

points_json.example: 'Surgery has a 90% survival rate' convinces far more patients than 'surgery has a 10% mortality rate.'
points_json.point: Framing effects: identical options produce opposite choices depending on wording. Gains trigger risk-aversion (take the sure thing); losses trigger risk-seeking (gamble to avoid the certain loss). Context, not math, decides.

points_json.example: A shopper drives across town to save 50 on a 200 jacket, but won't bother saving 50 on a 20,000 laptop.
points_json.point: We judge by proportions, not absolute amounts — diminishing sensitivity. The same 50 feels huge against 200 and trivial against 20,000, though the money is identical.

points_json.example: Once you own a concert ticket, you refuse to sell it for double what you paid — though you would never have bought it at that price.
points_json.point: The endowment effect: merely owning something inflates its value in our minds. Loss aversion makes giving up 'ours' painful — which is why free trials and test drives sell so effectively.

points_json.example: Employees stay in worse jobs and customers keep worse subscriptions simply because changing feels risky.
points_json.point: Status quo bias: we prefer current states even when alternatives are better. Combined with loss aversion, it explains brand loyalty, political inertia, and why organ-donor rates depend on the default checkbox.

points_json.example: People buy extended warranties for tiny risks but skip flood insurance for catastrophic ones.
points_json.point: The certainty effect: we overweight outcomes that are certain and underweight merely probable ones. A guaranteed small win beats a likely big win — and a possible disaster gets ignored until it strikes.

points_json.example: A poker player on tilt chases losses with wilder bets, abandoning all strategy.
points_json.point: Under real risk, emotions hijack calculation: fear breeds excessive caution, while the pain of losses breeds reckless gambling to 'get even.' Recognizing your reference point is the first defense.

summary: Why smart people make predictably irrational choices — prospect theory, loss aversion, and the framing tricks that steer decisions.
title: Decision Making Under Risk

points_json.example: A man must decide whether to steal an expensive drug to save his dying wife — the druggist refuses to lower the price.
points_json.point: Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma probes moral reasoning, not the answer. What matters is the justification: avoiding punishment (preconventional), upholding law and order (conventional), or appealing to universal principles (postconventional).

points_json.example: A child says stealing is wrong 'because you'll get punished'; a teen says it's wrong 'because it's against the law.'
points_json.point: Kohlberg's three levels: preconventional (morality = consequences for me), conventional (morality = social rules and approval), postconventional (morality = abstract principles like justice). Most adults reason mainly at the conventional level.

points_json.example: Gilligan argued Kohlberg's stages were built on male reasoning — and missed an entire moral voice.
points_json.point: Gilligan's care ethics: women often reason morally through relationships and responsibility rather than abstract rights. The debate reshaped moral psychology toward including care, not just justice.

points_json.example: Is it okay to push one person off a bridge to stop a trolley killing five? Most say no — though they'd pull a lever for the same trade.
points_json.point: The trolley problem reveals moral reasoning is not pure math: pushing feels worse than pulling a lever, though outcomes match. Physical contact, intention, and personal agency weigh heavily in moral judgment.

points_json.example: People strongly condemn harmless taboo violations — then cannot explain why when pressed.
points_json.point: Moral dumbfounding (Haidt): we feel something is wrong before we can say why, then invent reasons afterward. This supports the social intuitionist model — moral judgment is mostly fast intuition, with reasoning as press secretary.

points_json.example: Soldiers, judges, and doctors all show that training and culture reshape moral intuitions over time.
points_json.point: Moral reasoning develops: education, perspective-taking, and diverse experience push reasoning upward. But stress, disgust, and tribal loyalty can drag anyone's moral judgment down in the moment.

points_json.example: Whistleblowers who report corruption at great personal cost usually cite principle, not calculation.
points_json.point: Postconventional reasoners are rare but historically pivotal — figures like Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. acted on universal principles against law and custom. Kohlberg saw this as morality's highest stage.

summary: How we decide right from wrong — Kohlberg's stages, the Heinz dilemma, the trolley problem, and why gut feelings beat logic.
title: Moral Reasoning and Dilemmas

points_json.example: You recognize an old school friend instantly in a crowded market, though you haven't seen her in ten years.
points_json.point: Face recognition is a specialized brain skill. The fusiform face area (FFA) responds selectively to faces, and damage here causes prosopagnosia — face blindness — while other vision stays normal.

points_json.example: A prosopagnosic man fails to recognize his own wife at a party, identifying her only by her voice.
points_json.point: Prosopagnosia shows faces are processed separately from objects. Some people are born with it; others acquire it through brain injury. Oliver Sacks wrote movingly about navigating life without face recognition.

points_json.example: Turn a photo of a face upside down and it becomes strangely hard to recognize — far harder than an inverted house.
points_json.point: The face inversion effect: turning faces upside-down disrupts recognition much more than inverting other objects. Faces are processed holistically — as wholes — and inversion shatters that template.

points_json.example: Witnesses identify own-race faces far more accurately than other-race faces.
points_json.point: The own-race bias (cross-race effect) is one of psychology's most replicated findings, with serious legal consequences. Experience sculpts the face system: we become experts at faces we see most.

points_json.example: Newborns, minutes old, prefer looking at face-like patterns over scrambled ones.
points_json.point: Face preference is present at birth, suggesting an inborn bias. Within months, babies specialize: they narrow from recognizing all faces (even monkeys') to mainly human faces of their own race.

points_json.example: Airport passport officers vary enormously — a few 'super-recognizers' almost never err.
points_json.point: Super-recognizers sit at the opposite extreme from prosopagnosia, identifying faces with extraordinary accuracy. Police forces now recruit them for CCTV and crowd work.

points_json.example: Cover the top half of two identical face-halves aligned differently, and the bottom halves look different.
points_json.point: The composite face effect proves holistic processing: we cannot help fusing face parts into a whole. Misaligned halves break the illusion — the signature of configural face perception.

summary: The brain's face department — the fusiform face area, prosopagnosia, super-recognizers, and why upside-down faces baffle us.
title: Face Perception and Recognition

points_json.example: Two lines of identical length look different when one has outward-pointing arrows and the other inward ones.
points_json.point: The Müller-Lyer illusion: arrow fins distort length judgment. The carpentered-world hypothesis says people raised among rectangular buildings fall for it most — some non-Western groups barely see the illusion at all.

points_json.example: Two identical circles look different sizes when one is ringed by large circles and the other by small ones.
points_json.point: The Ebbinghaus (Titchener) illusion shows size is judged relative to surroundings. Remarkably, your hand opening to grasp the circle is accurate even while your eyes are fooled — vision-for-action resists the illusion.

points_json.example: Stare at a waterfall for a minute, then look at rocks — they appear to drift upward.
points_json.point: The motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) reveals direction-selective neurons: staring fatigues 'downward' detectors, so the balanced 'upward' detectors dominate afterward. Aristotle noticed this 2,300 years ago.

points_json.example: The two table tops in Shepard's illusion look completely different — yet they are identical parallelograms.
points_json.point: Shepard's tables demonstrate how powerfully 3D interpretation overrides 2D reality. The visual system prioritizes a coherent scene over accurate measurement — usually a good trade.

points_json.example: An Ames room makes a child look like a giant next to a tiny adult.
points_json.point: The Ames room exploits size-distance scaling: a trapezoidal room viewed from one peephole looks rectangular, so identical-height people appear vastly different sizes. Hollywood used it for forced-perspective effects.

points_json.example: Escher's impossible triangle looks buildable until you trace its edges and find the contradiction.
points_json.point: Impossible objects (Penrose triangle) show vision constructs locally consistent pieces without checking global coherence. Each corner looks fine; only the whole is impossible.

points_json.example: Illusions are not failures — they reveal the shortcuts of a system optimized for survival, not measurement.
points_json.point: The deeper lesson: perception is intelligent guessing. Illusions expose the brain's assumptions — about light, distance, and context — that make everyday vision fast and usually correct.

summary: Why your eyes lie to you — Müller-Lyer, Ebbinghaus, the Ames room, and what illusions reveal about how vision really works.
title: Visual Illusions Explained

points_json.example: Hold a finger before your nose and close each eye alternately — the finger jumps against the background.
points_json.point: Retinal disparity: each eye sees a slightly different image. The brain fuses them into one 3D view — stereopsis. Random-dot stereograms prove depth can emerge from disparity alone, with no other cues.

points_json.example: A coin held at arm's length looks tiny; the same coin near your face looks huge — yet you know its size never changed.
points_json.point: Monocular cues work with one eye: linear perspective (rails converge), occlusion (near objects block far ones), texture gradient, relative size, and height in the visual field. Painters have exploited these for centuries.

points_json.example: Look out a train window: nearby poles whip past while distant mountains barely move.
points_json.point: Motion parallax is a powerful depth cue — closer objects move faster across the retina. Babies, animals, and even insects use it. It is why the moon seems to follow your car.

points_json.example: Two flashing lights in sequence look like one light moving back and forth.
points_json.point: The phi phenomenon: still images shown rapidly create motion — the basis of cinema and animation. Beta movement and stroboscopic motion are its cousins; your brain invents the movement between frames.

points_json.example: As you walk forward, the visual world streams outward from the point you are heading toward.
points_json.point: Optic flow tells you where you are going and how fast. Pilots land using the expanding flow pattern; drivers brake by its rate. Gibson built his ecological theory of perception around it.

points_json.example: An adult and child standing together far away project tiny images — yet you perceive them as normal-sized people.
points_json.point: Size constancy: the brain scales retinal size by perceived distance. Emmert's law quantifies it — afterimages look bigger when projected on distant walls. Without constancy, the world would pulse with every step.

points_json.example: Virtual reality headsets must get vergence and accommodation right, or users feel sick within minutes.
points_json.point: Depth cue conflicts cause VR sickness: the eyes converge on virtual distance but focus on the near screen. Engineers battle this vergence-accommodation conflict — applied perception science in action.

summary: How flat retinal images become a 3D world — binocular and monocular cues, the phi phenomenon, and why VR makes people queasy.
title: Depth and Motion Perception

points_json.example: Sunlight, shade, and lamplight change the wavelengths bouncing off an apple — yet it always looks red.
points_json.point: Color constancy: the brain discounts the illuminant and perceives stable surface colors. Without it, every cloud would repaint the world. The visual system judges relative wavelengths, not absolute ones.

points_json.example: Stare at a green flag for 30 seconds, then look at white paper — a red flag appears.
points_json.point: Afterimages support Hering's opponent-process theory: color works in opposing pairs (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white). Fatiguing the green system leaves red dominant — a prediction the older trichromatic theory alone cannot make.

points_json.example: The Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory says three cone types (red, green, blue) mix to create all colors.
points_json.point: Both classic theories are right at different stages: three cone types in the retina (trichromatic), then opponent-process channels in later neural stages. Modern color science unites them.

points_json.example: About 8% of men confuse reds and greens — traffic lights are designed with position as backup.
points_json.point: Color blindness is usually red-green, inherited on the X chromosome (hence more common in men). True total color blindness is extremely rare. Most color-blind people see a rich world, just with fewer distinctions.

points_json.example: In 2015 the internet erupted: is the dress blue-black or white-gold?
points_json.point: The dress revealed individual differences in color constancy — whether your brain assumes the dress sits in shadow (discounting blue) or bright light. It became the most studied photograph in vision science.

points_json.example: Rods handle night vision (no color); cones handle daylight and color — which is why the world goes grey at dusk.
points_json.point: The duplex retina: 120 million rods for dim light, 6 million cones for color and detail. The fovea packs only cones — stare directly at a faint star and it vanishes, because the fovea is night-blind.

points_json.example: Advertisers, painters, and UI designers all exploit the fact that surrounding colors change how a color looks.
points_json.point: Simultaneous contrast: a grey square looks darker on white, lighter on black. Color is never perceived in isolation — context is part of the sensation itself.

summary: The science of seeing red — trichromatic and opponent-process theories, color blindness, afterimages, and the dress that broke the internet.
title: Color Vision

points_json.example: Students who studied with background music performed no better than those in silence — the 'Mozart effect' vanished under scrutiny.
points_json.point: The 1993 Mozart effect — ten minutes of Mozart temporarily boosting spatial scores — shrank to a brief arousal effect. Any stimulating, enjoyable sound does the same. There is no magic in Mozart specifically.

points_json.example: A song from a school trip instantly returns the bus, the jokes, the feeling of that exact day.
points_json.point: Music is a potent memory cue: melodies bind to autobiographical memories through emotion. Alzheimer's patients who cannot name family members can often still sing songs from their youth.

points_json.example: A catchy jingle loops in your head for hours, unstoppable and maddening.
points_json.point: Earworms (involuntary musical imagery) affect most people weekly. They are triggered by recent, repetitive, simple tunes — and chewing gum or solving puzzles can dislodge them by occupying the phonological loop.

points_json.example: A musician with absolute pitch names any note instantly — 'that's an F sharp' — without a reference tone.
points_json.point: Absolute pitch is rare (about 1 in 10,000), partly genetic and partly requiring early musical training. Most musicians use relative pitch — and compose masterpieces without absolute pitch.

points_json.example: Some people cannot tell if someone sings out of tune — they have amusia, or tone deafness.
points_json.point: Congenital amusia affects about 4% of people: a brain-based difficulty with pitch, not a lack of effort. Yet most amusics enjoy music's rhythm and emotion normally.

points_json.example: Years of musical training enlarge auditory and motor brain areas and strengthen connections between hemispheres.
points_json.point: Musicians' brains show real plasticity: larger corpus callosum, enhanced auditory cortex. Training transfers modestly to language and executive skills — though claims of big IQ boosts are overstated.

points_json.example: A sad song in a minor key with slow tempo reliably makes listeners feel melancholy across cultures.
points_json.point: Music hijacks emotion circuits: tempo, mode, and timbre map onto feelings with surprising universality. The brain releases dopamine at musical peaks — the same reward chemical as food and love.

summary: What music does to the mind — the Mozart effect myth, earworms, absolute pitch, and why melodies unlock lost memories.
title: Music and Cognition

points_json.example: Glance at scattered coins and instantly know there are three — without counting.
points_json.point: Subitizing: humans instantly perceive quantities up to about four without counting. Beyond that, we estimate. This ancient system is shared with many animals and infants.

points_json.example: Which is larger: 27 dots or 32 dots? You answer correctly without counting — approximately.
points_json.point: The approximate number system lets us compare magnitudes intuitively. Its precision — the Weber fraction — predicts later math achievement in children, suggesting math builds on this gut sense.

points_json.example: People respond faster to small numbers with the left hand and large numbers with the right.
points_json.point: The SNARC effect reveals a mental number line: small numbers live on the left, large on the right (reversed in right-to-left reading cultures). Abstract numbers are mapped onto space in the brain.

points_json.example: A bright child who cannot tell whether 7 is bigger than 5, despite normal intelligence otherwise.
points_json.point: Dyscalculia — number blindness — affects 5–7% of people: a core deficit in number sense, not laziness. Like dyslexia for words, it needs targeted intervention, not just more practice.

points_json.example: Children worldwide count on fingers — and banning it can actually harm early math learning.
points_json.point: Finger counting is cognitively valuable: fingers provide a physical number line that scaffolds arithmetic. Brain imaging shows finger areas activate even in adults doing mental math.

points_json.example: Rats press levers a set number of times; crows distinguish quantities; bees count landmarks.
points_json.point: Numerical ability is evolutionarily ancient: many species discriminate quantities, supporting survival decisions about food and predators. Human symbolic math is built atop this animal foundation.

points_json.example: A student who panics at math tests scores far below her true ability — anxiety consumes working memory.
points_json.point: Math anxiety is real and measurable: worry occupies the working memory needed for calculation. Expressive writing before tests and reframing anxiety as excitement measurably improve scores.

summary: The brain's number sense — subitizing, the mental number line, dyscalculia, and why animals can count too.
title: Numerical Cognition

points_json.example: A skilled reader recognizes the word 'house' instantly, without sounding out h-o-u-s-e.
points_json.point: The dual-route model: familiar words are read by the direct lexical route (whole-word recognition); new words use the phonological route (sounding out). Brain damage can knock out one route while sparing the other.

points_json.example: Children who can segment 'cat' into c-a-t learn to read far faster than those who cannot.
points_json.point: Phonological awareness — hearing the sounds inside words — is the strongest predictor of reading success. Phonics instruction, which teaches letter-sound links explicitly, beats whole-language approaches in large studies.

points_json.example: A bright 8-year-old reads haltingly, guesses wildly at words, and dreads reading aloud.
points_json.point: Dyslexia is a brain-based difficulty with accurate, fluent word reading, affecting 5–10% of children. It is not about reversed letters or low intelligence — it is a phonological processing difference with genetic roots.

points_json.example: Brain scans show dyslexic readers underactivate left-hemisphere reading areas — but targeted tutoring normalizes the pattern.
points_json.point: The dyslexic brain can be rewired: intensive phonological training changes brain activation toward typical patterns. Early intervention works best, but older readers improve too.

points_json.example: English-speaking children take years longer to master reading than Italian children.
points_json.point: Orthographic depth matters: transparent spellings (Italian, Finnish) are learned quickly; deep, irregular English slows everyone down and makes dyslexia more visible. The writing system shapes the reading brain.

points_json.example: Speed-reading courses promise 1,000 words per minute with full comprehension — controlled tests show comprehension collapses.
points_json.point: The speed-reading myth: eye movements physically limit reading speed, and 'reading' at 1,000 wpm is skimming. Comprehension, not eye speed, is the real bottleneck.

points_json.example: A dyslexic student who listens to audiobooks while following the text builds vocabulary most readers never reach.
points_json.point: Accommodations work with the brain, not against it: text-to-speech, extra time, and structured literacy programs let dyslexic learners thrive — many become exceptional scientists, artists, and entrepreneurs.

summary: How the brain learns to read — the dual-route model, why phonics wins, what dyslexia really is, and the speed-reading myth.
title: Reading and Dyslexia

points_json.example: To memorize a shopping list, picture milk flooding your front door, eggs hatching on the sofa, bread as your pillow.
points_json.point: The method of loci — the ancient memory palace — places vivid images along a familiar route. Memory champions memorize decks of cards this way. Bizarre, exaggerated images stick far better than dull ones.

points_json.example: Students tested on material a week later remember far more than students who only re-read it.
points_json.point: The testing effect: retrieving information strengthens it more than restudying. Every successful recall rewires the memory trace. Self-testing is the single most underused study technique.

points_json.example: Three 20-minute sessions across three days beat one 60-minute cram session for the same material.
points_json.point: The spacing effect (Ebbinghaus): distributed practice dramatically outperforms massed practice. Spaced repetition software schedules reviews at the optimal moment — just before you would forget.

points_json.example: Linking 'mitochondria' to 'mighty tiny powerhouses' beats repeating the word ten times.
points_json.point: Elaborative encoding: connecting new facts to existing knowledge, asking 'why' and 'how,' creates multiple retrieval routes. The deeper the processing, the stronger the memory.

points_json.example: Medical students remember anatomy better when they teach it to a peer than when they highlight textbooks.
points_json.point: The protégé effect: teaching forces organization, gap-finding, and clear explanation. Study groups where members teach each other outperform solo highlighting — which barely helps at all.

points_json.example: Sleeping after learning consolidates memories — students who sleep remember more than those who stay awake.
points_json.point: Sleep is a memory tool: the brain replays and consolidates learning during deep sleep. All-nighters sabotage the very memories being studied. Even short naps after learning help.

points_json.example: Exercise grows new neurons in the hippocampus — fit students show measurably better memory.
points_json.point: Aerobic exercise boosts BDNF, a growth factor for memory neurons. Regular exercise, good sleep, and spaced retrieval form the evidence-based trio for a stronger memory.

summary: Evidence-based ways to remember more — the memory palace, testing effect, spacing, and why sleep beats all-nighters.
title: Memory Improvement Techniques

points_json.example: A 70-year-old solves crossword puzzles slower than at 40, but gives wiser advice about life problems.
points_json.point: Fluid intelligence (solving new problems, processing speed) declines from the twenties. Crystallized intelligence (knowledge, vocabulary, wisdom) keeps growing into old age — the classic Cattell-Horn distinction.

points_json.example: An older driver takes longer to react at intersections but has fewer accidents than a reckless teenager.
points_json.point: Processing speed slows with age — the most universal cognitive change. But experience compensates: older adults use knowledge and caution to match or beat younger performance in real-world tasks.

points_json.example: A grandmother forgets why she entered a room, yet recalls her wedding day in vivid detail.
points_json.point: Working memory and prospective memory (remembering to do things) decline most. Long-term knowledge stays strong. Forgetting names and appointments is normal aging — rapidly worsening confusion is not.

points_json.example: Bilingual, educated, socially active elders show dementia symptoms years later than isolated peers.
points_json.point: Cognitive reserve: education, complex work, and social engagement build neural backup systems. Reserve does not prevent brain aging but delays its visible effects — use it or lose it has real science behind it.

points_json.example: Older adults remember the gist of stories better than exact details — and give better summaries.
points_json.point: Aging shifts memory style toward gist over verbatim detail. This is adaptive: schemas and wisdom improve while rote precision fades. Older judges and doctors often outperform juniors on complex decisions.

points_json.example: Normal aging: misplacing keys. Warning sign: putting keys in the freezer and not recognizing them later.
points_json.point: Distinguishing normal aging from dementia matters: normal aging is slower retrieval with intact recognition; dementia brings disorientation, personality change, and lost daily skills. Early assessment helps enormously.

points_json.example: Elders who learn new skills — photography, quilting, a language — show measurable cognitive gains.
points_json.point: The best anti-aging prescription: aerobic exercise, novel learning, social connection, and vascular health (blood pressure, diet). Crossword puzzles alone do little — novelty and challenge are what count.

summary: How thinking changes with age — fluid vs crystallized intelligence, cognitive reserve, and the difference between normal aging and dementia.
title: Cognitive Aging

points_json.example: People rate a job candidate as warmer after holding a hot cup of coffee versus an iced drink.
points_json.point: Embodied cognition: the body shapes thought. Physical warmth primes social warmth — metaphors like 'warm person' are not just language but lived bodily associations influencing judgment.

points_json.example: Students who gesture while explaining a math problem solve it better than those who sit still.
points_json.point: Gestures are not just communication — they help thinking itself. Encouraging gesturing improves problem-solving and learning; restricting hands measurably worsens performance.

points_json.example: Holding a pen between your teeth (forcing a smile) makes cartoons seem funnier.
points_json.point: The facial feedback hypothesis: expressions influence emotions, not just reflect them. Botox patients who cannot frown report milder negative moods — though the effect sizes are small and debated.

points_json.example: Expansive 'power poses' were claimed to raise testosterone and confidence — massive studies failed to replicate the hormone claims.
points_json.point: A cautionary tale: power posing shows how embodied effects can be overhyped. The honest lesson is that some body-mind links are real but small, and replication matters more than exciting headlines.

points_json.example: Baseball players judge a ball as bigger when they are hitting well — perception tracks ability.
points_json.point: Action shapes perception: the same hill looks steeper to a tired hiker; tools feel like body extensions. What the body can do changes what the eyes see.

points_json.example: Reading 'she grasped the idea' activates hand-movement brain areas — metaphors are bodily.
points_json.point: Conceptual metaphor theory (Lakoff): abstract thought borrows from bodily experience — we 'grasp' ideas, feel 'down,' move 'forward' in life. Language reveals the body's role in abstract reason.

points_json.example: Walking meetings produce more creative ideas than sitting meetings in controlled studies.
points_json.point: Practical payoff: movement aids creativity, standing desks sustain attention, and acting out concepts helps learning. The mind is not a computer in a vat — it thinks with the whole body.

summary: Thinking with the whole body — how warmth, gestures, and posture shape judgment, and the power-posing cautionary tale.
title: Embodied Cognition

points_json.example: A chatbot writes a convincing essay about grief — without ever having felt anything.
points_json.point: The Turing test (1950): if a machine converses indistinguishably from a human, should we call it intelligent? Modern chatbots pass casual versions — yet passing the test and understanding remain different things.

points_json.example: Searle imagined a man in a room following rulebooks to answer Chinese messages perfectly — understanding nothing.
points_json.point: The Chinese Room argument: symbol manipulation is not understanding. A system can produce perfect outputs with zero comprehension — a lasting challenge to claims that AI truly 'thinks.'

points_json.example: Neural networks were directly inspired by neurons — layers of simple units learning from examples.
points_json.point: Cognitive science birthed AI: neural networks copy the brain's architecture loosely. But artificial neurons are vastly simpler, and training on billions of words differs profoundly from a child's learning.

points_json.example: A child learns the word 'dog' from a handful of examples; AI needs millions of labeled images.
points_json.point: Human learning is sample-efficient and causal: children infer rules from tiny data and ask 'why.' AI excels at pattern-matching huge datasets but struggles with the flexible, one-shot learning toddlers do effortlessly.

points_json.example: Hiring AIs trained on historical data learned to prefer male resumes — amplifying past discrimination.
points_json.point: AI inherits human biases from its training data. Cognitive psychology's lessons about bias apply doubly to machines: they systematize and scale whatever prejudices the data contains.

points_json.example: Chess engines calculate millions of positions; grandmasters recognize meaningful patterns instantly.
points_json.point: Different intelligences: AI wins through brute-force search and statistics; humans win through intuition, analogy, and understanding. Each reveals the other's nature by contrast.

points_json.example: Studying AI failures — like confidently hallucinating false facts — illuminates human cognition too.
points_json.point: The deepest value is mirror-like: building thinking machines forces precise theories of thinking. Every AI limitation maps a question about what human understanding really is.

summary: What thinking machines teach us about thinking — the Turing test, the Chinese Room, and why children still outlearn supercomputers.
title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Thinking
